Topics.Title: The Agent–Environment Model
Topics.Summary: Defines agents, sensors, actuators, percepts, and percept sequences, and explains how an agent function maps perceptions to actions. Establishes the closed loop between an agent and the environment it inhabits.

Elements.Title: What Is an Agent?
Elements.BodyText: An agent is anything that can perceive its environment through sensors and act upon that environment through actuators. This simple definition applies equally to humans, robots, and software programs.
Elements.Notes: Examples: a human agent uses eyes and ears as sensors and hands and legs as actuators; a robotic agent uses cameras and infrared range finders with motors; a software agent receives keystrokes, file contents, and network packets and acts by writing files, displaying output, and sending packets.

Items.Text: Sensors supply the agent with information about the state of the world.
Actuators are the means by which the agent changes the state of the world.
The agent concept is a tool for analysis, not a precise classification of devices.
Almost any system can be viewed as an agent if we specify its sensors, actuators, and environment.

Elements.Title: Percepts and Percept Sequences
Elements.BodyText: A percept is the agent's perceptual input at any given instant, while the percept sequence is the complete history of everything the agent has ever perceived. Both are central to describing agent behaviour.
Elements.Notes: In the classic vacuum-cleaner world, a percept might be [A, Dirty] — the current location and whether it contains dirt.

Items.Text: An agent's choice of action at any instant can depend on the entire percept sequence observed to date.
It cannot depend on anything the agent has not perceived.
If the agent has memory, it can retain past percepts; without memory, only the current percept is available.
Tabulating behaviour over all possible percept sequences fully characterises an agent, though such tables are usually infinite.

Elements.Title: The Agent Function and the Agent Program
Elements.BodyText: The agent function is the abstract mathematical mapping from percept sequences to actions, and the agent program is the concrete implementation that runs on the agent's architecture.
Elements.Notes: Agent = architecture + program. The architecture is the physical or computational platform with sensors and actuators; the program decides what to do given percepts.

Items.Text: The agent function f maps every possible percept sequence to an action: f: P* → A.
The agent function is an external, abstract description of behaviour.
The agent program is the internal, finite implementation that produces that behaviour.
A table-driven program is one possible implementation but is impractical for all but trivial tasks.
Different programs can realise the same agent function with very different efficiency.

Elements.Title: The Perception–Action Loop
Elements.BodyText: The agent and environment form a closed loop: the environment generates percepts, the agent selects an action, and the action changes the environment, producing the next percept.

Items.Text: Each cycle consists of perceive, decide, and act.
Actions taken now influence the percepts received later, so decisions have consequences over time.
The loop continues indefinitely or until a terminal condition is reached.
Because the loop is continuous, an agent's behaviour must be evaluated over sequences of states, not single moments.

Elements.Title: Example: The Vacuum-Cleaner World
Elements.BodyText: A simple two-square vacuum world illustrates the agent–environment model concretely and is often used to compare alternative agent functions.
Elements.Notes: Environment: squares A and B, each either Clean or Dirty. Actions: Left, Right, Suck, NoOp.

Items.Text: The agent perceives its current location and whether that location is dirty.
One simple agent function is: if the current square is dirty, Suck; otherwise, move to the other square.
The same agent function could be implemented by a lookup table or by a few lines of code.
Varying the environment or the percept detail changes which agent function performs best.

Topics.Title: Rationality and Performance Measures
Topics.Summary: Explains what makes behavior rational: selecting the action expected to maximize a performance measure given the percept sequence and built-in knowledge. Distinguishes rationality from omniscience, perfection, and success.

Elements.Title: Defining a Rational Agent
Elements.BodyText: A rational agent selects, for each possible percept sequence, the action that is expected to maximize its performance measure. This definition ties rationality to four specific ingredients rather than to intelligence in a vague sense.
Elements.Notes: Russell and Norvig's standard definition frames rationality as expected performance maximization, not guaranteed good outcomes.

Items.Text: Rationality depends on the performance measure that defines the criterion of success.
It depends on the agent's prior knowledge of the environment.
It depends on the actions the agent is able to perform.
It depends on the agent's percept sequence to date — everything it has perceived so far.
Change any one of these four factors and the rational action may change.

Elements.Title: Performance Measures Evaluate Outcomes, Not Behavior
Elements.BodyText: A performance measure is an objective criterion that scores the sequence of environment states produced by the agent's actions. It is specified by the designer, not chosen by the agent.
Elements.Notes: Example: for a vacuum agent, 'amount of dirt cleaned in 8 hours' rewards dumping and re-cleaning dirt; 'having a clean floor at each time step' is a better measure.

Items.Text: Measure the effect on the environment, not how impressive the agent's internal behavior looks.
Design the measure according to what you actually want in the environment, not how you think the agent should act.
Poorly chosen measures invite degenerate strategies that score well while failing the real goal.
Measures may combine multiple criteria, such as speed, safety, cost, and comfort, often with trade-offs.

Elements.Title: Rationality Is Not Omniscience
Elements.BodyText: An omniscient agent knows the actual outcome of its actions in advance; a rational agent only maximizes expected performance given available information. Omniscience is impossible in reality.
Elements.Notes: Classic example: you cross a street after looking both ways, and a cargo door falls from a passing airplane and flattens you. Crossing was still rational.

Items.Text: Rationality is judged against expected outcomes, given the percepts received so far.
Unforeseeable events that cause a bad outcome do not make the prior decision irrational.
Agents are evaluated on the decision process available at the time, not with hindsight.
Demanding perfection would make rational design impossible in any uncertain environment.

Elements.Title: Rationality Versus Perfection and Success
Elements.BodyText: Rationality maximizes expected performance, while perfection would maximize actual performance. A rational agent can fail and an irrational agent can get lucky.

Items.Text: Success is an outcome; rationality is a property of the decision-making process.
A rational choice can produce a poor result when the environment behaves unexpectedly.
Lucky outcomes from careless choices do not retroactively make those choices rational.
Judging agents only by results would penalize sound reasoning under uncertainty.

Elements.Title: Information Gathering, Learning, and Autonomy
Elements.BodyText: Rational behavior includes actions that improve future percepts and knowledge, not just actions that pay off immediately. This extends rationality over time.
Elements.Notes: Looking both ways before crossing is information gathering; a vacuum agent that maps dirt patterns over time is learning.

Items.Text: Information gathering — such as exploration or looking before acting — is often a rational action because it raises expected future performance.
A rational agent should learn from its percepts to correct or extend its prior knowledge.
An agent is autonomous to the extent it relies on its own experience rather than solely on the designer's built-in knowledge.
An agent that ignores evidence contradicting its built-in assumptions lacks autonomy and becomes less rational over time.

Elements.Title: Rationality Is Relative to the Task Environment
Elements.BodyText: The same behavior can be rational in one environment and irrational in another, because rationality is always assessed against a specific setting and measure.
Elements.Notes: A vacuum agent that moves left and right forever is rational if dirt reappears and movement is free, but irrational if moves are penalized and the floor stays clean.

Items.Text: Change the performance measure and the optimal policy changes.
Change the environment's dynamics, such as whether dirt reappears, and the rational action changes.
Limits on the agent's actuators and sensors constrain which actions can be rational.
This dependency motivates specifying tasks explicitly before designing an agent.

Topics.Title: Specifying Tasks with PEAS
Topics.Summary: Introduces the PEAS framework—Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors—as a disciplined way to specify an agent's task before design. Walks through worked PEAS specifications for agents such as a vacuum cleaner, automated taxi, and medical diagnosis system.

Elements.Title: Why Specify the Task Before Designing the Agent
Elements.BodyText: Before choosing an agent architecture or algorithm, the designer must state precisely what problem the agent is solving. PEAS provides a disciplined checklist for that specification.
Elements.Notes: Skipping task specification often leads to agents that optimise the wrong thing or assume sensors and actuators that do not exist.

Items.Text: The agent program depends entirely on the task environment it must operate in.
A written specification exposes hidden assumptions about what the agent can perceive and do.
It makes competing designs comparable because they target the same stated task.
It forces the designer to state success criteria rather than discover them after deployment.

Elements.Title: The Four Elements of PEAS
Elements.BodyText: PEAS stands for Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, and Sensors. Together these four components fully describe the task an agent faces.
Elements.Notes: A common ordering convention is to write the performance measure first, because it constrains what counts as a good design for the other three.

Items.Text: Performance measure: the criterion that defines success in the agent's behaviour.
Environment: the surroundings and context in which the agent operates.
Actuators: the means by which the agent acts upon the environment.
Sensors: the means by which the agent perceives the environment.
All four must be stated together; changing any one changes the design problem.

Elements.Title: Writing a Good Performance Measure
Elements.BodyText: The performance measure is the hardest and most consequential part of a PEAS specification because it defines rationality for the agent.
Elements.Notes: Example pitfall: rewarding a vacuum agent for dirt collected lets it dump dirt back on the floor and re-vacuum it. Reward a clean floor instead.

Items.Text: Measure outcomes in the environment, not the agent's internal satisfaction with its own behaviour.
Specify what you actually want, not how you imagine the agent should achieve it.
Poorly chosen measures invite reward hacking and degenerate strategies.
Multiple objectives may need weighting, for example speed versus safety versus fuel use.

Elements.Title: Worked Example: Vacuum Cleaner Agent
Elements.BodyText: The simple vacuum world illustrates PEAS at its smallest scale.

Items.Text: Performance measure: amount of floor cleaned, cleanliness maintained over time, energy and time consumed, noise generated.
Environment: rooms or squares, dirt, obstacles, furniture, and floor surfaces.
Actuators: wheels or motors for movement, suction mechanism, brushes.
Sensors: dirt detector, bump or obstacle sensor, location sensor.

Elements.Title: Worked Example: Automated Taxi Driver
Elements.BodyText: The automated taxi shows how PEAS scales to a complex, open-ended real-world task.
Elements.Notes: Note how many competing objectives appear in the performance measure, which is typical of real applications.

Items.Text: Performance measure: safe arrival, legality, passenger comfort, trip time, fuel cost, and profit.
Environment: roads, traffic, pedestrians, weather, traffic signals, and other vehicles.
Actuators: steering, accelerator, brake, indicators, horn, and display or voice output.
Sensors: cameras, radar or lidar, speedometer, GPS, odometer, engine sensors, and a keyboard or microphone for passenger input.

Elements.Title: Worked Example: Medical Diagnosis System
Elements.BodyText: A diagnosis agent shows that PEAS applies equally to software agents with no physical body.
Elements.Notes: Here actuators and sensors are screens, keyboards, and data feeds rather than motors and cameras — a useful reminder that embodiment is not required.

Items.Text: Performance measure: accuracy of diagnosis, patient health outcomes, minimised cost, and avoidance of harmful treatments.
Environment: patients, hospital staff, medical records, and test facilities.
Actuators: display of questions, tests, diagnoses, treatment plans, and referrals.
Sensors: keyboard or form entry of symptoms, patient answers, and laboratory test results.

Elements.Title: Applying PEAS in Practice
Elements.BodyText: PEAS is a reusable template that turns a vague problem statement into an engineering specification.
Elements.Notes: Try writing PEAS descriptions for agents such as a part-picking robot, a refinery controller, an interactive English tutor, or a satellite image analyser.

Items.Text: Start with the performance measure, then derive what the agent must perceive and do to optimise it.
Check that every listed actuator and sensor is justified by the performance measure.
Revisit the specification when the environment changes, since new conditions may require new sensors.
A completed PEAS description feeds directly into classifying the task environment and selecting an agent architecture.

Topics.Title: Classifying Task Environments
Topics.Summary: Covers the key dimensions used to characterize task environments: fully vs. partially observable, deterministic vs. stochastic, episodic vs. sequential, static vs. dynamic, discrete vs. continuous, and single- vs. multi-agent. Shows how each property constrains the difficulty of the task.

Elements.Title: Why Classify Task Environments?
Elements.BodyText: Before designing an agent, we characterize the environment it must operate in, because environment properties determine which agent architectures and algorithms are viable. The classification is applied to the task environment as specified by PEAS, not to the agent itself.
Elements.Notes: The same physical world can yield different classifications depending on how the task is framed — e.g., chess with a clock is dynamic, chess without one is static.

Items.Text: Environment properties act as design constraints that rule in or out particular agent designs.
Harder environments generally require internal state, models, learning, or search over long horizons.
The dimensions are largely independent, so environments are described by a combination of labels.
Classification depends on how the task is defined, including the agent's sensors and actuators.
Real-world environments typically fall at the hard end of most dimensions.

Elements.Title: Fully vs. Partially Observable
Elements.BodyText: An environment is fully observable if the agent's sensors give it access to the complete state of the environment relevant to choosing an action at each point in time. Otherwise it is partially observable.
Elements.Notes: An environment can also be unobservable if the agent has no sensors at all, in which case it must act on a fixed plan.

Items.Text: Full observability means the agent need not maintain any internal state to track the world.
Partial observability arises from noisy or inaccurate sensors, or from parts of the state simply not being sensed.
Chess with a visible board is fully observable; poker and automated driving are partially observable.
Partially observable environments require the agent to keep a belief state or internal model of the hidden parts.
A vacuum agent with only a local dirt sensor cannot see the other square, making its world partially observable.

Elements.Title: Deterministic vs. Stochastic
Elements.BodyText: An environment is deterministic if the next state is completely determined by the current state and the action executed by the agent; otherwise it is stochastic.
Elements.Notes: Nondeterministic is sometimes distinguished from stochastic: nondeterministic environments list possible outcomes without probabilities, while stochastic ones attach probabilities.

Items.Text: Deterministic environments allow the agent to predict outcomes exactly and plan with certainty.
Stochastic environments force the agent to reason about probabilities and handle unexpected results.
Taxi driving is stochastic because traffic, weather, and tyre blowouts cannot be predicted.
A simple grid vacuum world with reliable actions is deterministic.
If an environment is deterministic except for the actions of other agents, it is often called strategic.

Elements.Title: Episodic vs. Sequential
Elements.BodyText: In an episodic environment the agent's experience is divided into independent atomic episodes, where each episode's action does not affect later episodes. In a sequential environment, current decisions can affect all future decisions.

Items.Text: Episodic tasks let the agent decide each case in isolation without looking ahead.
A defect-detection robot on an assembly line classifies each part independently, an episodic task.
Chess and taxi driving are sequential because early moves have long-term consequences.
Sequential environments require search, planning, or lookahead over sequences of actions.
Episodic environments are simpler because the agent does not need to think ahead.

Elements.Title: Static vs. Dynamic
Elements.BodyText: A static environment does not change while the agent is deliberating, whereas a dynamic environment can change during the agent's decision-making time. A semi-dynamic environment does not change, but the agent's performance score does.

Items.Text: Static environments remove time pressure, letting the agent deliberate as long as needed.
Dynamic environments require the agent to act in real time and treat inaction as a choice.
Crossword puzzles are static; taxi driving is dynamic because traffic keeps moving.
Chess played with a clock is semi-dynamic, since the clock penalises slow deliberation.
Dynamic environments force the agent to continuously re-sense the world as plans may become stale.

Elements.Title: Discrete vs. Continuous
Elements.BodyText: This distinction applies to the state of the environment, the way time is handled, and the agent's percepts and actions. Discrete environments have a finite or countable set of distinct states and actions; continuous ones range over real values.
Elements.Notes: The discrete/continuous distinction can apply differently to states, time, percepts, and actions within the same task.

Items.Text: Chess has a discrete set of board states and a finite set of legal moves per turn.
Taxi driving is continuous in state and time, with steering angle and speed varying smoothly.
Continuous domains usually require discretisation, approximation, or specialised numeric methods.
Camera input is technically discrete pixels but is often modelled as continuous intensities and positions.
Discrete environments allow exhaustive enumeration of states and actions, which continuous ones do not.

Elements.Title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent
Elements.BodyText: A single-agent environment contains only the agent in question, while a multi-agent environment contains other entities whose behaviour must be modelled as agents maximising their own performance measures. Multi-agent settings are further split into competitive and cooperative.
Elements.Notes: Randomised behaviour can be rational in competitive multi-agent settings, because unpredictability prevents opponents from exploiting you.

Items.Text: An entity counts as an agent if its behaviour is best described as maximising a performance measure that depends on your actions.
Chess is competitive multi-agent: one agent's success means the other's failure.
Taxi driving is partially cooperative, as drivers share the goal of avoiding collisions, and partially competitive for parking spaces.
A crossword puzzle is single-agent because no other entity's goals interact with the solver's.
Multi-agent environments introduce communication, negotiation, and game-theoretic reasoning.

Topics.Title: Applying Environment Properties to Real Tasks
Topics.Summary: Practices classifying familiar domains—chess, poker, driving, image classification, robot navigation—along every environment dimension. Connects environment type to the agent architecture and techniques best suited to it.

Elements.Title: A Checklist for Classifying Any Task Environment
Elements.BodyText: Before designing an agent, run the task through every environment dimension in a fixed order so no property is overlooked. The resulting profile directly constrains which agent architectures are viable.
Elements.Notes: Use the same six-to-seven question checklist every time: observability, agent count, determinism, episodicity, dynamics, discreteness, and knowledge of the environment.

Items.Text: Ask: can the sensors see the full state, or only part of it?
Ask: are there other agents whose behaviour affects the performance measure, and are they cooperative or competitive?
Ask: does the next state follow uniquely from the current state and action, or is there stochastic or unmodelled variation?
Ask: are decisions independent episodes, or do they commit the agent to future consequences?
Ask: does the world change while the agent deliberates, and are states, time, and actions discrete or continuous?
Record the answers as a profile, then match that profile to candidate agent designs.

Elements.Title: Chess and Poker: Observability and Opponents
Elements.BodyText: Classic board and card games are the cleanest illustration of how a single property change alters the required technique. Chess and poker share most properties but differ sharply in observability.
Elements.Notes: Chess with a clock is semi-dynamic: the board does not change while you think, but your remaining time does.

Items.Text: Chess is fully observable, deterministic, sequential, static (or semi-dynamic with a clock), discrete, and multi-agent competitive.
Poker is partially observable because opponents' hole cards are hidden, and stochastic because of the shuffle.
Chess supports minimax and alpha-beta search over a known game tree.
Poker requires belief states over opponent hands, probabilistic reasoning, and mixed (randomised) strategies to avoid exploitation.
Both are sequential, so neither can be solved by a reflex agent that ignores history.

Elements.Title: Automated Driving: The Hard Case
Elements.BodyText: Driving is the standard example of an environment that is difficult on nearly every dimension at once. It explains why autonomous vehicles need such elaborate architectures.
Elements.Notes: PEAS for driving: performance = safety, legality, speed, comfort, fuel use; environment = roads, traffic, pedestrians, weather; actuators = steering, throttle, brake, signals; sensors = cameras, LiDAR, radar, GPS, odometry.

Items.Text: Partially observable: occlusions, blind spots, and the unknown intentions of other drivers.
Stochastic: tyre slip, pedestrian behaviour, and weather defeat exact prediction.
Sequential and dynamic: the world keeps moving while the planner computes, so latency is a safety constraint.
Continuous in state, time, and action, and multi-agent with both competitive and cooperative elements.
Requires sensor fusion, probabilistic state estimation, continuous control, and online replanning rather than offline search.

Elements.Title: Image Classification: An Episodic, Static Environment
Elements.BodyText: Supervised perception tasks sit at the easy end of several dimensions, which is why they are amenable to pure learning pipelines. Each decision is self-contained.
Elements.Notes: Contrast with video tracking or active vision, where the agent chooses where to look next and the task becomes sequential.

Items.Text: Episodic: classifying one image has no effect on the next image presented.
Static: the image does not change while the model computes its output.
Deterministic from the agent's side, though label noise can make the mapping effectively stochastic.
Single-agent, with no adversary unless adversarial examples are considered.
Episodic structure means no planning or internal state is needed, so a feed-forward learned classifier suffices.

Elements.Title: Indoor Robot Navigation: Partial Observability Meets Continuity
Elements.BodyText: Mobile robotics combines noisy sensing, continuous spaces, and a changing world, making it a good bridge between game-like and real-world tasks.
Elements.Notes: Techniques that follow directly from this profile: particle filters or Kalman filters for localisation, occupancy grids for mapping, and sampling-based planners such as RRT for continuous motion.

Items.Text: Partially observable: range sensors see only nearby surfaces, so the robot must maintain a belief over its pose.
Stochastic: wheel slip and sensor noise make the outcome of a motion command uncertain.
Sequential: each move changes which parts of the map can be reached and observed next.
Dynamic if people or doors move, and continuous in pose, velocity, and time.
Typically single-agent, but becomes multi-agent cooperative in warehouse fleets requiring coordination.

Elements.Title: From Environment Profile to Agent Architecture
Elements.BodyText: The classification exercise is only useful if it changes the design decision. Each property maps to a concrete architectural requirement.
Elements.Notes: A useful rule of thumb: the harder the environment on each axis, the more internal machinery the agent needs and the less a simple reflex rule can achieve.

Items.Text: Partial observability forces an internal state or belief state, ruling out simple reflex agents.
Stochasticity pushes the agent from plans toward policies and expected-utility maximisation.
Sequential structure requires lookahead search, planning, or reinforcement learning rather than one-shot mapping.
Dynamic environments impose real-time deadlines, favouring anytime algorithms and reactive layers.
Continuous spaces require function approximation, sampling, or discretisation instead of exhaustive enumeration.
Multi-agent settings demand opponent modelling, game-theoretic reasoning, or explicit communication protocols.

Elements.Title: Common Classification Pitfalls
Elements.BodyText: Learners frequently misclassify environments by confusing the agent's limitations with the world's properties. Watching for these traps makes the analysis reliable.
Elements.Notes: When in doubt, ask whether the uncertainty is in the world or merely in the agent's model of it — the design consequence is often the same, but the reasoning differs.

Items.Text: Deterministic versus stochastic is judged from the agent's viewpoint: an unmodelled but lawful world is treated as stochastic.
Episodic does not mean short — a long task is still sequential if early actions constrain later ones.
Fully observable does not mean the agent knows everything; opponent intentions and future events remain unknown.
Known versus observable are distinct: the rules of poker are known while the state is only partially observable.
Semi-dynamic environments (chess with a clock) are easy to mislabel as fully static.

Topics.Title: From Specification to Agent Design
Topics.Summary: Links PEAS specifications and environment classification to choices among simple reflex, model-based, goal-based, utility-based, and learning agents. Reinforces how a well-defined task description drives rational agent construction.

Elements.Title: From PEAS Specification to Design Decisions
Elements.BodyText: A completed PEAS description is not merely documentation; it is the input that drives architectural choices for the agent. Each PEAS component constrains what the agent must compute and store.
Elements.Notes: Example: For an automated taxi, PEAS = Performance (safety, legality, speed, comfort, profit); Environment (roads, traffic, pedestrians, weather); Actuators (steering, accelerator, brake, horn, display); Sensors (cameras, LIDAR, speedometer, GPS, odometer).

Items.Text: The performance measure defines the objective function the agent must maximize, suggesting whether goals or utilities are needed.
The environment description reveals partial observability, uncertainty, and the presence of other agents.
The actuator list bounds the agent's action space and the granularity of its decisions.
The sensor list determines what the percept sequence contains and therefore what can be inferred directly versus inferred through internal state.
Any gap between what the sensors reveal and what the performance measure requires must be bridged by internal reasoning.

Elements.Title: Simple Reflex Agents: When Percepts Are Enough
Elements.BodyText: Simple reflex agents select actions using condition-action rules applied to the current percept alone, with no memory of the past. They are the cheapest and fastest design but only work under narrow conditions.
Elements.Notes: A vacuum agent that senses [location, dirty?] and applies 'if dirty then Suck' is a classic example.

Items.Text: Appropriate when the environment is fully observable, so the current percept determines the correct action.
Work well in episodic environments where past episodes do not affect the current decision.
They fail in partially observable settings, often causing infinite loops or repeated mistakes.
Randomizing actions can escape some loops but is not a substitute for internal state.
If PEAS analysis shows sensors cannot reveal the full state, this design should be rejected.

Elements.Title: Model-Based Agents: Handling Partial Observability
Elements.BodyText: When sensors do not reveal the full state, the agent must maintain internal state that tracks the unobserved parts of the world. This requires a model of how the world evolves and how actions affect it.
Elements.Notes: A self-driving car cannot see vehicles in its blind spot at every instant, so it maintains a tracked belief about their positions.

Items.Text: Internal state is updated from the percept history rather than the latest percept alone.
A transition model captures how the world changes independently and in response to the agent's actions.
A sensor model describes how world states map to percepts.
Dynamic and stochastic environments reinforce the need for state tracking and uncertainty representation.
In multi-agent environments the model must also include other agents' likely behavior.

Elements.Title: Goal-Based Agents: Reasoning About the Future
Elements.BodyText: Some tasks cannot be solved by reacting to the present state; the agent must consider the consequences of action sequences. Goal-based agents add explicit goal information and use search or planning to reach it.
Elements.Notes: Route finding for a taxi: 'be at the airport' is a goal that requires planning a sequence of turns.

Items.Text: Goals are typically binary — a state either satisfies the goal or it does not.
Sequential environments make goal-based reasoning necessary, since current actions affect future options.
Search and planning let the agent evaluate hypothetical future states before acting.
Goal-based agents are more flexible because changing the goal changes behavior without rewriting rules.
They are slower than reflex agents, trading computation time for generality.

Elements.Title: Utility-Based Agents: Trading Off Competing Objectives
Elements.BodyText: When a performance measure involves multiple conflicting criteria or uncertain outcomes, binary goals are insufficient. Utility functions map states to a measure of desirability, enabling principled trade-offs.
Elements.Notes: A taxi's PEAS performance measure combines safety, speed, legality, comfort, and profit — these conflict, so a utility function is required.

Items.Text: Use a utility-based design when the performance measure lists several competing objectives.
Stochastic environments require maximizing expected utility rather than guaranteed goal achievement.
Utility functions let the agent choose among multiple goal-satisfying paths by preferring better ones.
The utility function should be an internalization of the externally defined performance measure.
Mis-specified utilities produce agents that score well internally but behave poorly by the true measure.

Elements.Title: Learning Agents: Operating in Unknown Environments
Elements.BodyText: When the environment is unknown or too complex to specify in advance, the agent must improve its own performance from experience. A learning agent wraps any of the previous architectures with components that adapt it over time.
Elements.Notes: Unknown environments are those where the agent lacks knowledge of outcomes of its actions and must discover them.

Items.Text: The performance element selects actions and corresponds to the whole agent described earlier.
The learning element makes improvements based on feedback from the critic.
The critic evaluates behavior against a fixed external performance standard.
The problem generator suggests exploratory actions that may be suboptimal now but informative later.
Learning is the preferred approach when PEAS analysis reveals an unknown, dynamic, or continuous environment.

Elements.Title: A Workflow for Designing Rational Agents
Elements.BodyText: Combining PEAS specification with environment classification produces a repeatable design procedure. The result is the simplest architecture that still behaves rationally for the task.
Elements.Notes: Rationality is relative to the specification: an agent is rational only with respect to its performance measure, prior knowledge, available actions, and percept sequence.

Items.Text: Step 1: Write the PEAS description, defining performance before anything else.
Step 2: Classify the environment along observability, determinism, episodicity, dynamics, discreteness, agency, and known/unknown dimensions.
Step 3: Choose the least complex agent type that satisfies the demands revealed by that classification.
Step 4: Add internal state, planning, utility, or learning components only where the task requires them.
Step 5: Evaluate the implemented agent against the original performance measure and revise the design.
A vague or incomplete PEAS specification propagates into an agent that optimizes the wrong thing.
